content.heading: 10.4 Classification of States and Periodicity
content.paragraph: The communication classes of a Markov chain have important properties that help determine whether the state vectors converge to a unique steady-state vector. These properties are studied in this section, and it will be shown that Examples 3, ﻿4, and ﻿5 in Section 10.2 are examples of all the ways that the state vectors of a Markov chain can fail to converge to a unique steady-state vector.
content.heading: Recurrent and Transient States
content.paragraph: One way to describe the communication classes is to determine whether it is possible for the Markov chain to leave the class once it has entered it.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Let $C$ be a communication class of states for a Markov chain, and let $j$ be a state in $C$. If there is a state $i$ not in $C$ and $k > 0$ such that the $(i,j)$-entry in $P^{k}$ is positive, then the class $C$ is called a transient class and each state in $C$ is a transient state. If a communication class is not transient, it is called a recurrent class and each state in the class is a recurrent state.

content.paragraph: Suppose that $C$ is a transient class. Notice that once the system moves from $C$ to another communication class $D$, the system can never return to $C$. This is true because $D$ cannot contain a state $i$ from which it is possible to move to a state in $C$. If $D$ did contain such a state $i$, then the transitive property of the communication relation would imply that every state in $C$ communicates with every state in $D$. This is impossible.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Consider the Markov chain on $\left\{ 1\text{,~}2\text{,~}3\text{,~}4\text{,~}5 \right\}$ studied in Example 4 in Section 10.3. Its transition diagram is given in Figure 1. Determine whether each of the communication classes is transient or recurrent.

image.alt: A transition diagram shows the transition through 5 states in forward and reverse directions.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The communication classes were found to be $\left\{ 1\text{,~}2 \right\}$, $\{ 3\}$, and $\left\{ 4\text{,~}5 \right\}$. First consider class $\{ 3\}$. There is a positive probability of a transition from state $3$ to state $2$, so applying the definition with $k = 1$ shows that class $\{ 3\}$ is a transient class. Now consider class $\left\{ 1,2 \right\}$. The probability of a one-step transition from either state $1$ or state $2$ to any of states $3$, $4$, or $5$ is zero, and this is also true for any number of steps. If the system starts in state $1$ or $2$, it will always stay in state $1$ or $2$. Class $\left\{ 1\text{,~}2 \right\}$ is thus a recurrent class. A similar argument shows that class $\left\{ 4\text{,~}5 \right\}$ is also a recurrent class.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Consider the random walk with reflecting boundaries studied in Example 2 in Section 10.3. Determine whether each of the communication classes is transient or recurrent.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: This Markov chain is irreducible: the single communication class for this chain is $\left\{ 1\text{,~}2\text{,~}3\text{,~}4\text{,~}5 \right\}$. By the definition, this class cannot be transient. Thus the communication class must be recurrent.

content.paragraph: The result of the preceding example may be generalized to any irreducible Markov chain.
Remark:All states of an irreducible Markov chain are recurrent.

Suppose that a reducible Markov chain has two transient classes $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ and no recurrent classes. Since $C_{1}$ is transient, there must be a state in $C_{2}$ that can be reached from a state in $C_{1}$. Since $C_{2}$ is transient, there must be a state in $C_{1}$ that can be reached from $C_{2}$. Thus all states in $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ communicate, which is impossible. Thus the Markov chain must have at least one recurrent class. This argument can be generalized to refer to any reducible Markov chain with any number of transient classes, which along with the previous remark proves the following.
Remark:Every Markov chain must have at least one recurrent class.

content.paragraph: In Examples 3 and 4, the states were ordered so that the members of each class were grouped together. In Example 4, the recurrent classes were listed first followed by the transient classes. This ordering was convenient, as it allowed for the use of partitioned matrices to determine the recurrent and transient classes. It is also possible to use block multiplication to compute powers of the transition matrix $P$ if the states are reordered in the manner done in Examples 3 and 4: the states in each communication class are consecutive, and if there are any transient classes, the recurrent classes are listed first, followed by the transient classes. A transition matrix with its states thus reordered is said to be in canonical form. To see how this reordering works, consider the following example.

content.heading: Periodicity
content.paragraph: A final way of classifying states is to examine at what times it is possible for the system to return to the state in which it begins. Consider the following simple example.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: A Markov chain on $\left\{ 1\text{,~}2\text{,~}3 \right\}$ has transition matrix
The transition diagram, which is shown in Figure3, is quite straightforward. The system must return to its starting point in three steps and every time the number of steps is a multiple of three.

image.alt: A directed graph with an equilateral triangle of vertices as 1, 2, and 3. The flow is from 1 to 2 with p as 1, from 2 to 3 with p as 1, and from 3 to 1 with p as 1.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: A Markov chain on $\left\{ 1\text{,~}2\text{,~}3\text{,~}4 \right\}$ has transition matrix

and the transition diagram shown in Figure 4. If the system starts in state $1$, $2$, or $3$, the system may return to its starting point in three steps or in four steps, and may return every time the number of steps is $3a + 4b$ for some non-negative integers $a$ and $b$. It can be shown that every positive integer greater than $5$ may be written in that form, so if the system starts in state $1$, $2$, or $3$, it may also return to its starting point at any number of steps greater than $5$. If the system starts in state $4$, the system may return to its starting point in four steps or in seven steps, and a similar argument shows that the system may also return to its starting point at any number of steps greater than $17$.

image.alt: A figure shows two equilateral triangles with a common base and two common vertices. The vertices of the first triangle are 1, 2, and 3. The vertices of the second triangle are 2, 3, and 4. The side 2 to 3 is the common base.

content.paragraph: In Examples 6 and 8, the time steps at which the system may return to its initial site are multiples of a number $d$: $d = 3$ for Example 6, $d = 2$ for Example 8. This number $d$ is called the period of the state, and is defined as follows.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The period $d$ of a state $i$ of a Markov chain is the greatest common divisor of all time steps $n$ such that the probability that the Markov chain that started at $i$ visits $i$ at time step $n$ is strictly positive.

content.paragraph: Using a careful analysis of the set of states visited by the Markov chain, it may be shown that the period of each state in a given communication class is the same, so the period is a property of communication classes. See Appendix 2 for a proof of this fact, which leads to the following definition.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The period of a communication class $C$ is the period of each state in $C$. If a Markov chain is irreducible, then the period of the chain is the period of its single communication class. If the period of every communication class (and thus every state) is $d = 1$, then the Markov chain is aperiodic.

content.paragraph: The reason that the greatest common divisor appears in the definition is to allow a period to be assigned to all states of all Markov chains. In Example 7, the system may return to its starting state after any sufficiently large number of steps, so the period of each state is $d = 1$. That is, the Markov chain in Example 7 is aperiodic. Notice that this chain does not exhibit periodic behavior, so the term aperiodic is quite apt. Using the definition confirms that the period of the Markov chain in Example 6 is $d = 3$, while the period of the Markov chain in Example 8 is $d = 2$. The next theorem describes the transition matrix of an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain.

note.title: Theorem 4
note.heading: Theorem 4
note.paragraph: Let $P$ be the transition matrix for an irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain. Then $P$ is a regular matrix.

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Let $P$ be an $n \times n$ transition matrix for an irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain. To show that $P$ is regular, a number $k$ must be found for which every entry in $P^{k}$ is strictly positive. Let $1 \leq i$, $j \leq n$. Since the Markov chain is irreducible, there must be a number $a$ that depends on $i$ and $j$ such that the $(i,j)\text{-element}$ in $P^{a}$ is strictly positive. Since the Markov chain is aperiodic, there is a number $b$ that depends on $j$ such that the $(j,j)\text{-element}$ in $P^{m}$ is strictly positive for all $m \geq b$. Now note that since $P^{a + m} = P^{a}P^{m}$, the $(i,j)\text{-element}$ in $P^{a + m}$ must be greater than or equal to the product of the $(i,j)\text{-element}$ in $P^{a}$ and the $(j,j)\text{-element}$ in $P^{m}$. Thus the $(i,j)\text{-element}$ in $P^{a + m}$ must be strictly positive for all $m \geq b$. Now let $k$ be the maximum over all pairs $(i,j)$ of the quantity $a + b$. This maximum exists because the state space is finite, and the $(i,j)\text{-element}$ of $P^{k}$ must be strictly positive for all pairs $(i,j)$. Thus every entry of $P^{k}$ is strictly positive, and $P$ is a regular matrix.

content.paragraph: Theorem 5 says that in the case of an irreducible Markov chain with period $d > 1$, the vector $\textbf{q}$ is the limit of the average of the probability vectors $P^{n + 1}\textbf{x}_{0}$, $P^{n + 2}\textbf{x}_{0}$, ... , $P^{n + d}\textbf{x}_{0}$. When a Markov chain is irreducible with period $d > 1$, the vector $\textbf{q}$ may still be interpreted as a vector of occupation times.
